entities.name: Jean d'Orléans-Longueville
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jean d'Orléans-Longueville, born into a powerful cadet branch of the French royal House of Valois, emerged as a prominent ecclesiastical figure in early 16th-century France, culminating in his brief but significant elevation to cardinal in 1533. His career, spanning from his appointment as Archbishop of Toulouse in 1503 to his death just months after receiving the red hat, exemplifies the intertwining of aristocratic lineage, political influence, and high clerical office characteristic of the pre-Reformation Catholic Church in France. As a scion of the ducal house of Longueville, a family deeply entrenched in royal service and military command, his ascent within the Church was both a reflection of his family's prestige and a strategic consolidation of their power through ecclesiastical patronage, linking him directly to the French monarchy and its diplomatic ambitions.

Jean's ecclesiastical career began with substantial appointments, notably becoming Archbishop of Toulouse in 1503, a major metropolitan see, followed by his elevation to Bishop of Orléans in 1521. These roles were often held in commendam, allowing him to collect revenues while potentially delegating spiritual duties to suffragans. His most significant, albeit short-lived, achievement was his creation as a cardinal by Pope Clement VII on March 10, 1533, receiving the title of Cardinal-Priest of Santi Silvestro e Martino ai Monti. This elevation occurred during a period of intense diplomatic maneuvering between France, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Papacy, underscoring the political dimension of high clerical appointments.

entities.summary:
Jean d'Orléans-Longueville, born in 1484 at the Château de Parthenay, was a prominent French prelate whose career exemplified the deep entanglement of aristocratic power, ecclesiastical office, and royal influence in late medieval and early modern France. As a scion of the powerful Orléans-Longueville ducal house, a cadet branch of the ruling Valois dynasty, his ascent through the Church hierarchy was less a spiritual calling and more a strategic consolidation of family prestige and political leverage. His brief but significant tenure as a cardinal of the Roman Catholic Church in 1533, though lasting only six months before his death, placed him at the nexus of Franco-Papal diplomacy during a period of intense religious and political flux across Europe.

His ecclesiastical career began early, secured by his noble lineage. He was appointed Archbishop of Toulouse in 1503, a major see in southern France, at the remarkably young age of 19. This was followed by his elevation to Bishop of Orléans in 1521, further cementing his influence in central France. Concurrently, he served as abbot in commendam of the prestigious Abbey of Bec, accumulating substantial revenues and patronage. These appointments illustrate a system where high Church offices were often distributed to secure loyalty, fund noble families, and extend royal authority, rather than solely for spiritual leadership. His cardinalate, conferred by Pope Clement VII in March 1533, was likely a diplomatic gesture aimed at strengthening ties between the Papacy and King Francis I of France, particularly as the king sought alliances amidst the burgeoning Protestant Reformation and the ongoing conflicts with the Habsburgs.
